modules.title: Python foundations
modules.summary: Use variables, collections, loops and functions to turn a question into a repeatable calculation.
lesson: A list stores an ordered collection. A dictionary maps unique keys to values. Choose the structure that matches your data.
Write small functions with explicit inputs and outputs. Test the empty input and the usual case before working with a larger dataset.
tasks: Write a function that computes total revenue from a list of prices.
Handle an empty list and explain your return value.

modules.title: Explore and clean data
modules.summary: Inspect a table, find missing values and build a documented cleaning process.
lesson: Start by checking shape, column types, missing values and duplicate keys. A missing value can mean unknown, unavailable or not applicable.
Avoid filling every missing value with zero. Decide using the meaning of the column and document what changed.
tasks: Load a CSV and produce a missing-value summary.
Create a cleaned copy and document three decisions.

modules.title: SQL for analysis
modules.summary: Filter, aggregate and join tables without losing sight of the grain of your data.
lesson: The grain describes what one row represents. Confirm the grain before a join so that repeated keys do not silently multiply your totals.
WHERE filters rows before aggregation. HAVING filters groups after aggregation. COUNT(column) excludes nulls; COUNT(*) counts rows.
tasks: Calculate revenue by customer using GROUP BY.
Compare row counts before and after joining an orders table.

modules.title: Statistics that explain
modules.summary: Describe variation, compare groups and communicate uncertainty.
lesson: The mean is sensitive to extreme observations. The median is often a useful companion when a distribution is skewed.
Correlation describes association, not causation. Confounding variables and selection effects can explain an apparent relationship.
tasks: Compare mean and median for a skewed price column.
Describe one conclusion your dataset cannot support.

modules.title: Visual storytelling
modules.summary: Choose a chart that answers a question and write an evidence-based takeaway.
lesson: Use bars for category comparisons and lines for time trends. A scatter plot helps inspect relationships between numeric variables.
Label units and show the relevant baseline. Write a title that makes the question clear and avoid implying precision the data does not support.
tasks: Create one comparison chart and one trend chart.
Add a takeaway and a limitation below each chart.

modules.title: Advanced SQL patterns
modules.summary: Use CTEs and window functions for rankings, running totals and comparisons.
lesson: GROUP BY collapses rows; a window function calculates across related rows while retaining each row. PARTITION BY defines the groups for a window.
Use explicit ordering for running calculations. Ties behave differently in ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK.
tasks: Rank customers by revenue within each region.
Calculate a running total with an explicit window frame.

modules.title: Build a useful dashboard
modules.summary: Turn a business question into a small, readable dashboard with defined metrics.
lesson: Define each metric, its time range and the decision it supports before choosing visuals. A dashboard should help someone decide what to do next.
Check filter behaviour and reconcile totals against a source query. A visually polished dashboard can still be wrong.
tasks: Define revenue, order count and average order value.
Build a dashboard and reconcile its totals to SQL.

modules.title: Experiments and decisions
modules.summary: Frame a hypothesis, choose a metric and recognise the limits of an experiment.
lesson: Choose a primary outcome and success criterion before observing results. Random assignment helps reduce confounding.
Statistical significance is not the same as practical value. Consider effect size, uncertainty and the cost of implementation.
tasks: Draft an experiment for a checkout change.
Specify a primary metric and a guardrail metric.

modules.title: Features and validation
modules.summary: Create a reproducible train/test split and prevent leakage.
lesson: Split data before fitting transformations. A preprocessing step fitted on all observations can leak information from the test set into training.
Choose validation that matches the problem: chronological splits for future prediction and group-aware splits for repeated entities.
tasks: Create a held-out test set and a preprocessing pipeline.
Identify one potential source of leakage.

modules.title: Train a baseline model
modules.summary: Compare a simple baseline with a model and choose a relevant evaluation metric.
lesson: A baseline establishes whether added complexity helps. Compare against a simple rule such as predicting the majority class or the training mean.
Accuracy alone can mislead when classes are imbalanced. Examine precision, recall and the confusion matrix in the context of error costs.
tasks: Fit a dummy baseline and a tree-based model.
Compare their performance using the same validation split.

modules.title: Explain model behaviour
modules.summary: Inspect errors by segment and communicate where a model should not be trusted.
lesson: An overall metric can hide poor performance on a subgroup. Inspect errors across meaningful segments and document small sample sizes.
Feature importance is a description of a fitted model, not evidence that changing a feature will cause the outcome to change.
tasks: Review five false predictions and group common errors.
Write a model card with limitations and intended use.

modules.title: Publish your evidence
modules.summary: Present a reproducible project with a clear question, evidence and limitations.
lesson: A useful README explains the problem, data source, setup, approach and findings. Include the exact command needed to reproduce the work.
Separate measured outcomes from hypothetical opportunities. Link your notebook or dashboard and acknowledge dataset limitations.
tasks: Publish a repository with a reproducible README.
Write three findings supported by a table or chart.

questions.prompt: Which collection maps unique keys to values?
questions.explanation: A dictionary stores key-value pairs; each key identifies one value.

questions.prompt: What does a function return if it reaches the end without a return statement?
questions.explanation: Python returns None when no explicit return value is supplied.

questions.prompt: What is the best first step before filling missing values?
questions.explanation: The meaning and pattern of missing data should guide the treatment.

questions.prompt: Which operation summarises revenue by region in pandas?
questions.explanation: Grouping by region and summing revenue creates one aggregate per region.
HAVING applies conditions to groups after aggregation.
COUNT(column_name) excludes null values. COUNT(*) counts rows.

questions.prompt: Which statistic is generally less sensitive to extreme outliers?
questions.explanation: The median depends on rank rather than the magnitude of extreme values.

questions.prompt: A strong correlation by itself establishes…
questions.explanation: Correlation measures association. A causal claim needs additional evidence.

questions.prompt: Which chart is a natural starting point for monthly revenue trends?
questions.explanation: A line chart displays ordered observations over time.

questions.prompt: How does a window function differ from GROUP BY?
questions.explanation: Window functions calculate over related rows without collapsing each group.

questions.prompt: When should a scaler be fitted?
questions.explanation: Fit preprocessing on training data and apply the learned transformation to other splits.

questions.prompt: For a rare positive class, what should accompany accuracy?
questions.explanation: Precision and recall help expose performance on the rare positive class.

questions.prompt: Feature importance proves a feature causes the outcome.
questions.explanation: Importance describes the model, not a causal intervention.

questions.prompt: What should happen before selecting dashboard charts?
options: Choose as many colours as possible
questions.explanation: Metric definitions and intended decisions determine what the dashboard needs to show.

questions.prompt: A statistically significant effect is always worth implementing.
questions.explanation: Practical value also depends on effect size, uncertainty, risks and implementation costs.

projects.title: Predict prices, explain errors
projects.summary: Build a regression baseline and investigate where it fails.
milestones: Document the dataset, target, units and intended use.
Create a train/test split and fit preprocessing on training data only.
Compare a dummy baseline and one model using MAE.
Inspect errors by segment and publish a model card.

Judgement: discuss historical data and deployment limits.

projects.title: Understand customer retention
projects.summary: Use SQL to compare customer cohorts and write a retention brief.
milestones: Define an eligible customer and a completed purchase.
Assign each customer a first-purchase cohort in SQL.
Calculate monthly retention with incomplete cohorts clearly labelled.
Publish a cohort chart and two testable follow-up hypotheses.

Quality: handle missing customer IDs and returns.

exercises.title: Revenue by customer
exercises.prompt: Given orders(customer_id, amount, status), return total paid revenue by customer, highest first. Exclude unpaid orders.
exercises.solution:
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'paid'
GROUP BY customer_id
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
exercises.explanation: Filter paid rows before aggregating. Group by customer and order by the computed sum.

exercises.title: Rank customers within regions
exercises.prompt: Given customer_sales(region, customer_id, revenue), add a dense rank within each region, with highest revenue first.
exercises.explanation: PARTITION BY restarts ranking for each region. DENSE_RANK gives tied revenues the same rank without gaps.

exercises.title: A reliable revenue function
exercises.prompt: Write total_revenue(prices) that returns the sum of a list of numeric prices and 0 for an empty list. Try [12, 8, 5] and [].
exercises.explanation: sum naturally handles an empty iterable. Add tests for decimals and negative adjustments if your use case allows them.

exercises.title: Audit missing values
exercises.prompt: For a pandas DataFrame df, calculate the percentage of missing values per column, sorted highest first.
exercises.starter:
import pandas as pd

# df is your loaded dataset
exercises.explanation: isna produces booleans. Their column mean is the missing proportion, which is converted to a percentage.
